title: Objects & Classes
blurb: Bundle state with behavior, speak the language of dunders, and inherit instead of rewriting — then prove it all through scripted drivers.

cells.title: Classes bundle state with the behavior that guards it
cells.body:
A class pairs data with the code allowed to touch it. The __init__ method runs once per object and establishes its starting state; every method receives that state as self. The payoff is not 'organization' — it is that rules about the data live in exactly one place. If a thermostat must reject settings outside 10..30, that check belongs in the method that sets the value, and then no other code path can forget it.

This is also the honest answer to 'parallel lists' code: instead of names[i], temps[i], modes[i] drifting out of sync, one object owns its name, temperature and mode together. When you feel yourself indexing three lists in lockstep, that is the moment a class is trying to happen. State + invariants + operations in one namespace is the whole idea.

cells.title: Dunder methods make objects speak Python
cells.body:
Double-underscore methods are how your object plugs into the language itself. Define __eq__ and 2 == 1-style comparisons consult your rule; define __lt__ and sorted(), min() and max() work on your objects with zero extra code; define __str__ and print() shows what you choose. You are not overriding syntax — you are filling in the hooks the built-ins were already calling.

The practical consequence for algorithmic work: comparison-driven algorithms (sorting, priority queues, binary search) are generic. Get __lt__ right and your Version or Job type slots into all of them. One rule to keep in mind: __lt__ must be a consistent ordering (if a < b and b < c then a < c), or the sort still 'works' but produces garbage — the dunder is a contract, not a suggestion.

cells.title: Inheritance: build on, don't rebuild — and test through drivers
cells.body:
Inheritance says 'a Square is a Rectangle with a tighter constructor', not 'these two classes feel similar'. The subclass reuses everything the parent does and changes only what differs — typically by calling super().__init__(...) and then adding or overriding behavior. If you cannot say the 'is-a' sentence out loud, prefer composition (one object holding another) over inheritance.

Because classes expose behavior rather than plain values, the practical testing pattern on this platform is the driver: a function that builds your objects, feeds them a scripted sequence of operations, and returns a plain list/string/number the tests can compare. The driver pattern mirrors how real test suites exercise stateful code — you assert on the observable trace of a session, not on the object's private internals.

exercise.title: The Crate Stack
exercise.statement:
A dock crane can only reach the top of a pile of crates: the last crate placed is the first one taken off. Model the pile as a class CrateStack with push(item), pop() (returning the top crate, or None when the pile is empty — never an exception), and size().

Then write the driver stack_run(ops), which is what the tests call. Each op is either the string "pop", the string "size", or a pair ["push", item]. The driver builds one CrateStack, replays the ops in order, and returns the flat list of values produced by the pops and size checks.
constraints: items may be strings, ints or any other value
pop on an empty pile returns None and the driver keeps going

examples.why: last-in-first-out, then one pop too many
size reports 1 after the push; the pop returns 1; then the pile is empty

hints: Which built-in list behavior already is a last-in-first-out pile? You mostly need to guard one operation.
Store the crates in a list; push appends, pop removes and returns the last element — but only after handling the empty case with None. size is len of the list.
In the driver, compare op to the strings 'pop' and 'size' first, otherwise it is a push pair and op[1] is the item. Append every pop/size result to out.
exercise.reasoning: The class exists to own one rule: the pile is last-in-first-out, and it can run empty. Both facts live in pop() — return the most recent item, or None when there is nothing — so no caller can get the underflow policy wrong. The driver, meanwhile, shows why we test stateful objects through a scripted trace: a single push or pop proves little, but the sequence (push two, pop three, push mid-sequence) forces the pile's behavior to be right at every step, and its flat output list is directly comparable. Designing the trace is the same skill as designing a regression test for any stateful component.

exercise.title: The Guarded Thermostat
exercise.statement:
A thermostat unit only accepts integer targets from 10 to 30 inclusive. Build a class Thermostat where both the constructor Thermostat(start) and the method set(value) raise ValueError for out-of-range targets; value() returns the current target. A rejected set leaves the previous target untouched.

Then write the driver thermostat_trace(start, ops) (what the tests call). It constructs Thermostat(start); if that raises, it returns ["invalid start"] immediately. Otherwise it replays ops — each op is ["set", v] or ["get"] — recording "ok" or "ValueError" for each set (caught, never crashing) and the current target for each get, and returns the list.
constraints: valid targets are the integers 10 through 30 inclusive
construction and set use the same rule; a bad start means the whole trace is invalid

examples.why: 99 is out of range so it is refused and the target stays 25

hints: If the constructor and set() must enforce the same rule, how do you write that rule exactly once?
Let __init__ just call self.set(start). set raises ValueError outside 10..30 and otherwise stores the target. The driver wraps each set in try/except and never lets the exception escape.
try: unit = Thermostat(start) except ValueError: return ["invalid start"]. Then per op: for set, try unit.set(v), appending 'ok' or 'ValueError'; for get, append unit.value().
exercise.reasoning: The design move is single-point validation: the constructor delegates to set(), so the range rule exists in exactly one method and the constructor cannot disagree with later updates. The driver then demonstrates the right way to live with a raising API: catch at the call site that has a recovery plan (record the refusal, keep going) and let everything else propagate. Two edge details matter: a rejected set must leave state untouched — which happens naturally because the assignment sits after the check — and an invalid start is a different outcome from an invalid set, so the driver reports them differently. Contracts that distinguish construction failure from update failure are much easier to build on.

exercise.title: Shape Ledger
exercise.statement:
A landscaping app bills plots by area and needs a small shape hierarchy. Define a base class Shape that declares the contract (name() and area()), a Rectangle(width, height) with area width * height, a Square(side) that inherits from Rectangle and reuses its constructor by calling super() with the side twice, and a Compound(a, b) holding two earlier-built shapes whose area is their sum. The names reported are exactly "rectangle", "square" and "compound".

Write the driver shape_report(specs) (the tested function). Specs are processed in order: ["rect", w, h], ["square", s], or ["compound", i, j] where i, j are indices of previously built shapes. It returns a list of strings "index:name=area" in build order.
constraints: compound indices always reference earlier entries (they may reference other compounds)
a shape may be reused in several compounds

examples.why: the compound combines shapes 0 and 1, so its area is 6 + 4

hints: Square differs from Rectangle only in how it is constructed. What is the smallest way to express that?
Square.__init__ calls super().__init__(side, side) and inherits area() unchanged. Compound holds the two shape objects it is given; its area() delegates to them.

In the driver, keep a built list; for each spec create the right object (Compound takes built[i] and built[j] — the objects themselves, not their indices). Append str(i) + ':' + name + '=' + str(area).
exercise.reasoning: The hierarchy earns its keep through two relationships. Square is-a Rectangle: it inherits area() untouched and only tightens construction — which is exactly when inheritance is the right tool (shared behavior, different initialization). Compound has-a pair of shapes: it stores the objects themselves, so its area() just delegates and adds — and because it depends only on the Shape contract, compounds of compounds work with no extra code. The driver is a tiny interpreter over specs, and the fact that its output is a list of plain strings is the driver-pattern lesson: rich object graphs are verified through their canonical, printable projections.

exercise.title: Version Sorting
exercise.statement:
A plugin manager must order versions written as "major.minor.patch", where missing parts count as zero: "2" means 2.0.0 and equals "2.0.0". Comparison is numeric per part — 1.9 < 1.10, exactly unlike text ordering — and the canonical text of a version always prints all three parts.

Implement a class Version(major, minor, patch) with __eq__ and __lt__ so that sorted() works on Version objects, plus __str__ rendering "major.minor.patch". Then write the tested driver version_sort(specs): parse each spec string into a Version, and return [sorted_strs, distinct] where sorted_strs is the list of str(v) in sorted order and distinct is the number of distinct versions (duplicates detected with ==).
constraints: each spec is 'a', 'a.b' or 'a.b.c' with integer parts 0..999, no leading zeros
sorted() must rely on your __lt__; duplicates must be detected via your __eq__
sorting is stable, so equal versions keep their input order in the output

examples.why: plain numeric ordering of three distinct versions
1.9 < 1.10 numerically, and '2' is canonically printed as 2.0.0

hints: What single piece of data decides both equality and order for a version? How do tuples already compare?
Store the three numbers and compare a key tuple (major, minor, patch) in both __eq__ and __lt__. The driver pads missing parts with zeros when parsing and prints via __str__.

parts = [int(p) for p in spec.split('.')]; pad with [0] * (3 - len(parts)). sorted(versions) needs only __lt__; count distinct by keeping a seen list and testing v == d for each — that path exercises your __eq__.
exercise.reasoning: Everything hinges on realizing that a version is a 3-tuple of numbers: tuples already compare lexicographically, so __eq__ and __lt__ both reduce to comparing (major, minor, patch) — one source of truth for the whole ordering, which is why it cannot disagree with itself. The 1.9 < 1.10 trap is what string sorting gets wrong and per-part numeric comparison gets right. The dunder payoff is structural: because sorted() calls __lt__, your type slots into the entire sorting machinery for free — and the distinct-count loop calls __eq__ directly, so both halves of the comparison protocol are actually exercised. Canonicalizing the string in __str__ (always three parts) keeps '2' and '2.0.0' printing identically after they compare equal.
